header_title: Time Dilation and the Light Clock

audio_script: A light clock works by bouncing a photon between two mirrors. If the clock is at rest, the photon travels straight up and down. But if the clock is moving sideways, the photon must travel along a diagonal path to catch the moving mirror. The diagonal is longer than the straight path. Since the speed of light is the same in every inertial frame, a longer path takes longer to traverse. So the moving clock ticks slower than the stationary one. This is time dilation. On screen, we plot the Lorentz factor gamma as a function of velocity as a fraction of the speed of light. At rest, gamma equals one. No dilation. At half the speed of light, gamma is about one point one five. At ninety percent of light speed, gamma is two point two nine. At ninety-nine percent, gamma is about seven. And as the velocity approaches c, gamma diverges to infinity. The curve has a vertical asymptote at v equals c. This is why no massive object can reach the speed of light. It would require infinite energy. A GPS satellite must correct for this effect many times per second to stay synchronized with Earth. Muons created high in the atmosphere survive to the ground only because their internal clocks tick slowly. Time dilation is not a philosophical curiosity. It is the geometry of space-time. Whenever two observers move relative to one another, they disagree about which events are simultaneous, and that disagreement is exactly what the gamma curve quantifies.

audio_script: Suppose a spaceship moves at half the speed of light relative to Earth, and inside it a probe is fired forward at half the speed of light relative to the ship. What is the probe's speed from Earth's frame? Newtonian physics would say one full light speed. But that answer is wrong. Velocities do not simply add in relativity. The correct formula is the sum of the two velocities, divided by one plus their product over c squared. For half and half, the numerator is one full c, and the denominator is one point two five. Dividing gives zero point eight c. Not c. Not more than c. This is the relativistic velocity addition formula. On screen, we plot the resulting speed as a function of one velocity, with the second velocity fixed at half c. The dashed red line marks the speed of light. Notice that the curve flattens against that line and never crosses it. Even if you set the first velocity to c itself, and then to c again, the sum remains c. The speed of light is invariant. It is the same in every frame. This is why the theory of relativity is called relativity. The invariant is not velocity. The invariant is the speed of light. Once you accept that, the entire geometry of space and time must shift, and velocity addition is just the first consequence. The formula has been verified countless times with fast-moving electrons, muons, and spacecraft. No laboratory experiment has ever observed a velocity above c.

tagline: Even at rest, mass stores energy
visual_data_json: [{"type": "text", "id": "title", "text": "Rest Energy: E Equals mc Squared", "pos": [0.0, 3.9, 0], "color": "#F2F3F5", "font_size": 30}, {"type": "energy_bar", "id": "rest_energy", "pos": [-3.2, 0.5, 0], "width": 4.5, "fill": 0.95, "label": "rest", "color": "#F1C40F"}, {"type": "energy_bar", "id": "kinetic", "pos": [3.2, 0.5, 0], "width": 4.5, "fill": 0.15, "label": "kinetic", "color": "#2ECC71"}, {"type": "text", "id": "caption", "text": "mass itself is energy, in a silent form", "pos": [0.0, -4.15, 0], "color": "#F1C40F", "font_size": 16}]
audio_script: Special relativity says that mass and energy are two names for the same thing. The equation is E equals m c squared. Energy equals mass times the speed of light squared. The speed of light is a huge number, three times ten to the eighth meters per second. Squaring it gives nine times ten to the sixteenth. So even a tiny mass corresponds to an enormous energy. A single gram of matter, if fully converted, would release nine times ten to the thirteenth joules. That is roughly the energy of a small nuclear weapon, or about twenty kilotons of TNT. Notice the numbers on screen. On the left, the rest energy bar fills almost the whole height. On the right, the kinetic energy of a slowly moving object is a tiny sliver by comparison. At everyday speeds, kinetic energy is negligible compared to rest energy. Only when an object moves at a significant fraction of light speed does the kinetic energy become comparable. This is why particle accelerators need enormous machines to push particles to near light speed. The rest energy of an electron is five hundred eleven thousand electron volts. The rest energy of a proton is nine hundred thirty eight million electron volts. The rest energy of a kilogram of any material is nine times ten to the sixteenth joules. This equivalence was first verified in 1932 by Anderson, who saw a positron annihilate with an electron and produce gamma rays. Today it powers nuclear reactors, radiometric dating, and every particle physics experiment in the world. Mass is energy in a very quiet form.

audio_script: Special relativity replaces separate ideas of space and time with a single geometry called space-time. On a space-time diagram, the horizontal axis is space and the vertical axis is time. Light travels at forty-five degrees. Why? Because a light ray covers one meter of space in exactly the time it takes light to travel one meter. If we measure both axes in the same units, light moves diagonally. Now consider an event happening at the origin. The set of all points a light ray could reach from that event traces two diagonal lines, one going up and to the right, one up and to the left. Those two rays, plus their mirror images going backward in time, form a double cone. This is the light cone. Everything inside the upper cone is in the future of the origin. Any signal that could have reached those points traveled slower than light. Any event inside the lower cone is in the past. Everything outside the cone is the elsewhere. No signal from the origin can reach there. No signal from there can reach the origin. Cause and effect live only inside the cone. This is why nothing can travel faster than light. If it could, it would leave the cone, and cause-and-effect ordering would break down. Two observers would disagree about whether A caused B. In a framework where the speed of light is fixed, the light cone is the boundary of the reachable universe. Every event you can ever influence, and every event that can ever influence you, lives inside your light cone. Everything else is permanently disconnected.

audio_script: In one dimension, angular momentum is just a number. Spin a wheel and it has a certain amount of it. But in three dimensions, angular momentum is a vector. It has a magnitude and a direction. The magnitude equals the moment of inertia times the angular velocity. The direction points along the axis of rotation, following the right-hand rule. Curl the fingers of your right hand in the direction of the spin, and your thumb points along the angular momentum vector. This is not arbitrary. The vector nature of angular momentum is what makes the gyroscope work. When you push on the axis of a spinning wheel, the angular momentum vector changes direction. That change is what produces precession. On screen, we see a spinning disk. The blue disk rotates. The green arrow shows the angular velocity vector, pointing up along the axis. The yellow arrow shows the angular momentum vector, also pointing up but longer, because it is I times omega. For this disk, mass two, radius one, so I is one. Spin rate two, so L is two. The magnitude is exactly the product. The direction is exactly the axis. When the axis changes, L changes. That change requires a torque, and torque equals the time derivative of L. This is the rotational version of Newton's second law. When there is no torque, L is conserved. That conservation is what keeps a top spinning upright, what keeps a gyroscope pointing north, and what makes a spinning figure skater stay vertical. Angular momentum is a vector because rotations have axes, and axes have directions.

audio_script: Two identical rods. Same mass, same length. One is pivoted at its center, the other at one end. They are the same physical object. But their moments of inertia are different. For a uniform rod about its center, the moment of inertia is one twelfth of mass times length squared. For the same rod about one end, it is one third of mass times length squared. That is four times larger. Why? The parallel-axis theorem tells us. The moment of inertia about any axis equals the moment of inertia about a parallel axis through the center of mass, plus mass times the distance squared between the two axes. For the end pivot, the distance from the center of mass to the end is half the length. So we add mass times half-length squared. That is one quarter of mass times length squared. Add it to one twelfth and you get one third. Four times larger. This is not a coincidence. It is a general theorem. It applies to any rigid body, any axis, any mass distribution. Whenever you know the moment of inertia about the center of mass, you can compute the moment of inertia about any parallel axis in one line. On the left, the rod rotating about its center. On the right, the same rod rotating about one end. Watch how much faster the end-pivoted rod sweeps out its angle. Same angular velocity, but the mass distribution is farther from the axis, and the parallel-axis theorem captures exactly how much extra inertia that adds. This is why the period of a pendulum depends on where along its length it is supported, and why a meter stick pivoted at the end swings slower than when pivoted at the middle.

tagline: Two masses, two springs, two frequencies

audio_script: Two masses on a spring. Each alone would oscillate at its own natural frequency. But when they are coupled, something new happens. The motion is no longer simple. Instead, it is a superposition of two normal modes. In the first mode, both masses move together. They do not stretch the spring at all. The frequency is just the natural frequency of one mass. In the second mode, the masses move oppositely. They compress and stretch the spring, and the frequency is higher. Every motion of this system is a sum of these two modes, with amplitudes and phases determined by the initial conditions. On screen, the animation is not a hand-drawn trajectory. It is the exact numerical solution of Newton's laws, integrated with a fourth-order Runge-Kutta solver at six hundred steps. Two masses, one spring, no damping. Mass A starts at rest, mass B starts with velocity zero point five. The spring pulls them together, then pushes them apart. Watch the two bodies. Sometimes they move together, sometimes oppositely. The energy transfers back and forth between the two modes. For a full oscillation, the pattern repeats. But it is not a simple sinusoidal motion. It is a combination of two sinusoids with incommensurate frequencies. This is the essence of normal modes. Any linear system with n degrees of freedom has n normal modes. Every motion is a sum. Find the modes, and you have solved the system. This is the reason Fourier analysis works, and why every vibrating structure in engineering can be decomposed into its modes.

tagline: Cosine is the shadow of a rotating vector

audio_script: Euler's formula is one of the most beautiful equations in mathematics. E to the i theta equals cosine theta plus i sine theta. It connects three seemingly unrelated things: the exponential function, trigonometry, and imaginary numbers. What does it mean? On a complex plane, e to the i theta is a point on the unit circle at angle theta. As theta increases, the point rotates counterclockwise around the circle at constant speed. The real part of the position is cosine theta. The imaginary part is sine theta. On screen, the yellow dot rotates around the circle. The dashed lines to the horizontal and vertical axes trace out the projections. On the right, we plot the real part of the position over time. It is a pure cosine. Watch as the rotating vector sweeps around the circle, its horizontal shadow traces the cosine curve exactly. The vertical shadow would trace the sine. This is not an approximation. It is exact. The magnitude of e to the i theta is always one. The derivative of e to the i theta with respect to theta is i times e to the i theta. That is a remarkable fact. Differentiating a complex exponential just multiplies it by i, which rotates it by ninety degrees. This is why complex exponentials are the natural language of wave physics. Every sinusoidal oscillation can be written as the real part of a complex exponential. Every derivative becomes a multiplication. Every differential equation becomes an algebraic equation. When you solve for electrical circuits, quantum wavefunctions, or sound waves, this is the tool. The imaginary unit is not a fudge. It is the algebra of rotations.

tagline: The envelope that silences a vibration

audio_script: Every real oscillator loses energy. Friction, air resistance, internal heating. The motion slowly dies out. This is damping. For small damping, the frequency is almost unchanged, but the amplitude decays exponentially. The envelope of the motion is e to the minus gamma t over two, where gamma is the damping rate. On the left, a mass on a spring. The green anchor is the pivot, and the blue mass oscillates. Watch the amplitude shrink over time. On the right, we plot the envelope as a function of time. The exponential falls from one toward zero. The actual motion oscillates inside this envelope. Every peak sits on the curve. Every trough as well. The rate of decay is governed by the ratio omega over gamma, which is called Q. A high Q means slow decay. A tuning fork has Q around one thousand. A quartz crystal has Q in the tens of thousands. An atomic transition has Q in the hundreds of millions. When damping is small, the frequency stays close to the undamped natural frequency. When damping is large, the frequency shifts. The formula is the square root of omega zero squared minus gamma squared over four. If gamma exceeds twice omega zero, the oscillation stops altogether. The system becomes overdamped. Instead of oscillating, it just creeps back to equilibrium. This is what you feel in a car with bad shock absorbers. The oscillation is not damped enough, and the car bounces. In a good car, the damping is tuned so the ride settles in about one cycle. This is the crossover between underdamped, critically damped, and overdamped. All three are contained in the same equation.

tagline: Any periodic shape is a sum of sines
visual_data_json: [{"type": "text", "id": "title", "text": "Fourier Synthesis", "pos": [0.0, 3.9, 0], "color": "#F2F3F5", "font_size": 34}, {"type": "harmonic_decomposition", "id": "fourier", "length": 7.0, "n_terms": 5, "color": "#4CC9F0"}, {"type": "text", "id": "caption", "text": "add one sine at a time, get a square", "pos": [0.0, -4.15, 0], "color": "#F1C40F", "font_size": 16}]
audio_script: Any periodic shape can be written as a sum of sines. This is Fourier's theorem, and it is one of the most powerful ideas in physics and engineering. The animation shows a square wave being built up from its harmonic components. Start with the fundamental: a simple sine that completes one cycle per period. Then add the third harmonic, three times the frequency, one third the amplitude. Then the fifth, one fifth the amplitude. Then the seventh. With each added term, the shape gets closer to a square. The corners sharpen. The flat top becomes flatter. The infinite sum is exactly the square wave. The amplitudes fall off as one over n, where n is the harmonic number. Only odd harmonics appear because the square wave is antisymmetric. The animation shows five terms. With fifty, the shape would be visually indistinguishable from a square. This is why a musical instrument sounds different depending on the shape of its waveform. A flute produces a nearly pure sine. A clarinet produces odd harmonics. A violin produces both odd and even. The ear hears these combinations as different tones. Every digital signal ever recorded is a finite Fourier sum. Every compressed image is a finite Fourier transform. Every resonant cavity, from a violin body to a laser, has its own set of harmonics. When you understand the modes, you understand the sound.

audio_script: A uniform rod of mass two kilograms and length two meters is pivoted about one end. What is its moment of inertia about that end? Directly, the answer is one third mass times length squared. That is one third times two times four, which is eight thirds, about two point six seven kilogram meters squared. Using the parallel-axis theorem, the moment of inertia about the center of mass is one twelfth mass times length squared, which is two thirds. audio_script: Euler's formula is e to the i theta equals cosine theta plus i sine theta. It connects the exponential function, trigonometry, and imaginary numbers. On a complex plane, e to the i theta is a point on the unit circle at angle theta. As theta increases, the point rotates around the circle. The real part is cosine. The imaginary part is sine.
